lead: A power screw turns rotary motion into straight-line motion by pushing a nut along a threaded shaft. The thread is an inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder, so the torque you apply must beat thread friction and lift the load. Screws raise car jacks, move machine slides, clamp work in a vice, and drive slow linear actuators. Some syllabi call this a translational screw.
prereq: You need: friction, torsion and combined stress (Unit 1, Foundations: Design Process and Stresses), and the thread terms from chapter 4.1.

sections.h3: The thread as an inclined plane

blocks.text: Unwrap one turn of the thread from the mean cylinder. The turn becomes a right triangle. The base is the circumference π d<sub>m</sub>; the height is the lead l. The angle between the slope and the base is the lead angle α.

d<sub>m</sub> is the mean diameter, the average of the major and minor diameters. l is the lead, the axial distance the nut moves in one turn. p is the pitch, the distance between adjacent threads. For a single-start thread l = p. For a double-start thread l = 2p, and so on. The mean diameter is not the nominal outside diameter.

blocks.where: α is the lead (helix) angle; l is the lead; d<sub>m</sub> is the mean diameter. Use the same units for l and d<sub>m</sub>.

blocks.text: Square, trapezoidal and Acme threads are common. A square thread has flat flanks and gives the simplest friction formula. A trapezoidal thread has angled flanks, usually 30° included. The Acme thread is the inch version with 29°. Angled flanks carry side loads better and are easier to cut.
For a square thread, the torque to raise the load is:
T<sub>r</sub> = (W d<sub>m</sub> / 2) × (μ + tan α) / (1 − μ tan α)
blocks.where: T<sub>r</sub> is raising torque in N·m; W is axial load in N; d<sub>m</sub> is mean diameter in m; μ is thread friction coefficient; α is lead angle.

blocks.text: To lower the load, the torque is:
T<sub>l</sub> = (W d<sub>m</sub> / 2) × (μ − tan α) / (1 + μ tan α)
blocks.where: T<sub>l</sub> is lowering torque in N·m; the other symbols are as above. If T<sub>l</sub> > 0, a torque must still be applied to lower the load: the screw is self-locking. If T<sub>l</sub> < 0 (that is, μ < tan α), the load runs the screw down by itself and the screw is overhauling; a brake or extra friction is needed to hold the load. T<sub>l</sub> = 0 at μ = tan α is the boundary.

blocks.text: That condition is self-locking. For a square thread it is μ ≥ tan α. A large friction coefficient or a small lead angle both help.
Efficiency is useful work out divided by work in: η = W l / (2π T<sub>r</sub>). With thread friction only, it becomes:
η = tan α (1 − μ tan α) / (tan α + μ)
blocks.where: η is efficiency (no unit); W l is useful work per turn; 2π T<sub>r</sub> is input work per turn. At small α the factor (1 − μ tan α) is near 1, but keep it in exams.

blocks.text: Collar friction adds T<sub>c</sub> = μ<sub>c</sub> W r<sub>c</sub>, where μ<sub>c</sub> is collar friction coefficient and r<sub>c</sub> is mean collar radius. Add T<sub>c</sub> to T<sub>r</sub>; efficiency falls because the same load needs more input work.

The screw body carries axial compression W and torsion T. At core diameter d<sub>c</sub>, direct stress is σ = W/A<sub>c</sub>, with A<sub>c</sub> = π d<sub>c</sub>²/4. Torsional shear is τ = 16T/(π d<sub>c</sub>³). For a ductile screw use σ<sub>eq</sub> = √(σ² + 3τ²) and compare with yield strength divided by factor of safety.
The nut threads share the load over z engaged threads. Bearing pressure is p = W/(π d<sub>m</sub> h z), where h is thread depth. Keep p below the allowable for the nut material.
A long screw in compression can buckle. Check slenderness and use Euler or Johnson formula. Short screws usually fail by thread shear or bearing before buckling.

figure.caption: Efficiency of a square thread with μ = 0.15 rises with lead angle over the plotted 0–20° range; it reaches a maximum near α ≈ 41° and then falls. The marked point is the worked screw at α = 4.55° and η = 0.342.

spec.aria: Efficiency rises with lead angle for a square thread with friction coefficient 0.15; the marked point is the worked screw at 4.55 degrees.

examples.question: A square-thread power screw has mean diameter d<sub>m</sub> = 24 mm, lead l = 6 mm, and raises a load W = 20 kN. The thread friction coefficient is μ = 0.15. Collar friction is neglected. Find the lead angle, the raising torque, the efficiency, and state whether the screw self-locks.
steps: Convert units: d<sub>m</sub> = 0.024 m, l = 0.006 m, W = 20 000 N.
μ = 0.15 and tan α = 0.07958, so μ > tan α. The screw is self-locking.
examples.answer: Lead angle α = 4.55°, raising torque T<sub>r</sub> = 55.8 N·m, efficiency η = 0.342 (34.2%), and the screw is self-locking.
examples.check:
import math
W = 20000.0
dm = 0.024
l = 0.006
mu = 0.15
tan_alpha = l / (math.pi * dm)
alpha = math.degrees(math.atan(tan_alpha))
T = W * dm / 2 * ((mu + tan_alpha) / (1 - mu * tan_alpha))
eta = tan_alpha * (1 - mu * tan_alpha) / (tan_alpha + mu)
print(round(alpha, 2))
print(round(T, 1))
print(round(eta, 3))

traps: Using nominal diameter d instead of mean diameter d<sub>m</sub> in tan α and torque. The mean is d<sub>m</sub> = (d + d<sub>c</sub>)/2, not the outside diameter.
Using pitch p in place of lead l. For a single-start thread they are equal; for a double-start thread l = 2p, so α and torque change.
Dropping the (1 − μ tan α) factor in efficiency when the lead angle is not small. At α = 4.55° it changes the third digit; in exams it can change the mark.

Forgetting collar friction. A collar adds T<sub>c</sub> = μ<sub>c</sub> W r<sub>c</sub> to the raising torque, so more input torque is needed and efficiency falls. Collar friction also resists the load running down, so a screw that overhauls with thread friction alone may become self-locking once the collar is included: the load runs down only if (W d<sub>m</sub>/2)(tan α − μ)/(1 + μ tan α) > μ<sub>c</sub> W r<sub>c</sub>.
Reading self-locking as 'small lead' only. For a square thread the test is μ ≥ tan α. A large μ or a small α both help.

quiz.q: Define lead and pitch of a thread. How are they related for a single-start screw?
quiz.a: Lead is the axial advance of the nut in one turn; pitch is the distance between adjacent threads. For a single-start screw, lead = pitch.

quiz.q: State the self-locking condition for a square-thread power screw.
quiz.a: The screw is self-locking when μ ≥ tan α, where μ is thread friction coefficient and α is lead angle.

quiz.q: Why does a power screw need a larger torque to raise a load than the ideal W l/(2π)?
quiz.a: The ideal value assumes no friction. The real torque must also overcome thread friction and, if present, collar friction, so the input work is larger.

quiz.q: A square screw has d<sub>m</sub> = 30 mm, l = 4 mm, μ = 0.12. Find α and tan α.
For the screw in the previous question, find the torque to raise W = 15 kN, neglecting collar friction.
A screw with α = 5° and μ = 0.06 is not self-locking. What happens when the load is released, and how can you make it self-locking without changing the load?
quiz.a: The load can run the screw down because μ < tan 5° = 0.0875. Increase friction — for example rougher flank finishes, a different nut material, or a poorer or no lubricant. Or reduce the lead to reduce α, or add a friction brake or collar so the load is held.

quiz.q: Why does a long power screw in compression need a buckling check even if the thread stresses are safe?
quiz.a: Axial compression can cause lateral deflection and sudden buckling. Slenderness decides whether Euler or Johnson applies. A stress check alone does not catch instability.

beyond: Not for the exam. Ball screws replace sliding thread friction with rolling balls and reach efficiencies above 90%, so they are common in CNC machine slides and 3D-printer axes. They are often preloaded to remove backlash, and they usually need a brake because they are not self-locking. Search 'ball screw recirculating', 'lead screw vs ball screw', and 'power screw buckling' for the next layer.
